background.definition: Human bite is a traumatic injury caused by human teeth. Bites are defined as "simple" or "occlusive". Clenched-fist injuries occur when a fist makes contact with teeth during a strike or assault, also called "fight bite".

list.listitem: Incidence is 45/100,000/year in a British population.
It is estimated that 250,000 human bites occur per year in the United States in both adults and children.
Mammalian bites account for 1% of emergency department visits; of those, human bites are the third most common (after dog and cat bites).
Assault.
Play.
Child abuse.
Domestic violence, particularly in some parts of Africa.
Self-injurious behavior, sometimes associated with Lesch-Nyhan syndrome.
Infections are frequently polymicrobial with aerobic pathogens (such as streptococci, Eikenella corrodens, and Staphylococcus aureus) and anaerobes (such as Fusobacterium and Peptostreptococcus).
Human bite wounds are associated with trauma to soft tissue or bone caused by crush or impact, as well as soft tissue infection.
The human bite wound infection rate is as high as 50% when it involves the hand. Bites from children are much less likely to cause infection.
Infection occurs when oral flora is transmitted into a wound that has penetrated the dermis.
Hand infections from bites may be more problematic as they can involve bones, metacarpophalangeal joints, tendons, tendon sheaths, and deep fascial spaces.
Ask specifically if a wound could have been caused by human teeth, particularly if the patient had been in a fight. C
Determine if the wound is high risk by assessing location (hands, feet, or over a joint capsule) and depth (beyond the epidermis). C

Ask specifically if the wound could have been caused by a human bite or contact with teeth. Patients may not initially describe an injury as such, but asking the question improves the case-detection rate and may prompt different treatment of the wound. This is especially true for patients who were in a fight and may have struck someone in the mouth with their fist ("fight bite").

Determine the time since the bite injury occurred, as wounds less than 24 hours old may be closed primarily, especially if a good cosmetic result is important. If the wound is more than 24 hours old, debridement and observation may be appropriate.
Obtain medical history, including allergies, tetanus immunization status, and current medications.

Examine the wound to determine the extent of penetration, specifically for extension beyond the epidermis, into a tendon or joint capsule, or into a fascial compartment. Note the presence of puncture wounds and any injury to underlying structures including bones, tendons, or joints.
Note evidence of infection including abscess, lymphadenopathy, skin erythema and induration, purulent wound drainage, or fever.
Evaluate for the presence of foreign bodies (such as retained teeth fragments).
Consider the possibility of child abuse when examining bite wounds in children.
No evidence exists that wound cultures affect the choice of antibiotics or improve outcomes.
Consider HIV, HBV, and HCV titers at baseline if the wound carries high risk.
Consider an x-ray of the wound to rule out fracture, bony involvement, and evaluate for the presence of foreign bodies (ie, tooth fragments).
Always ask patients specifically whether a wound could have been caused by human teeth. They may not wish to volunteer this information because of embarrassment or legal ramifications.
Ascertain the timing of the wound in relation to patient presentation.

Irrigate with tap water and debride the wound. Surgical debridement is recommended for wounds with delayed presentation, while primary closure is an option for carefully selected low-risk wounds for which a good cosmetic result is important.
Irrigate bite wound with copious tap water and debride devitalized tissue. C
Bites on the hands or feet, overlying a joint capsule, or those that penetrate the epidermis should be treated with 875 to 125 mg amoxicillin-clavulanic acid twice daily for 5 days. A
Surgical wound debridement may be required if there is delayed presentation (more than 1 day) in bite wounds to the hand. B
HIV prophylaxis is not routinely recommended. C

Prophylactic antibiotics may reduce the risk of infection after human bites. Low-risk bites that penetrate only the epidermis and do not involve hands, feet, skin overlying joints, or cartilaginous structures appear to have similar rates of infection regardless of whether antibiotics (cephalexin/penicillin combination) are used.

Use 875 to 125 mg amoxicillin-clavulanic acid orally twice daily for 5 days as the first-line choice for human bite prophylaxis. For patients with penicillin allergy, consider 450 mg clindamycin orally thrice daily or 500 mg metronidazole thrice daily plus either 500 mg ciprofloxacin orally twice daily, 400 mg moxifloxacin daily, or 100 mg doxycycline twice daily (see ).
Any patient who has not had a tetanus immunization in more than 5 years should be given a booster at the time of presentation.

While there have been case reports, the risk of HIV transmission is believed to be extremely low (much less likely from a bite than from a needlestick). HIV prophylaxis is not routinely recommended but may be considered on a case by case basis.

Copious irrigation with at least 1 L of fluid is accepted as standard of care though no evidence for this exists. Tap water is equivalent to saline or sterile water for preventing infection in traumatic wounds.
Debridement of devitalized tissue is also accepted as standard of care with subsequent wet-to-dry dressing changes until clean granulation tissue is noted.
Surgical wound debridement may be required if there is delayed presentation (more than 1 day) in bite wounds to the hand.
Primary wound closure may be acceptable in carefully selected low-risk wounds for which a good cosmetic result is important (eg, the face).
Do not close human bite wounds on hands and feet because of the high infection risk, especially wounds that involve joints, tendon sheaths, and deep spaces.
Primary wound closure is recommended for trunk and extremity wounds (excluding hands and feet) that are less than 12 hours old and head and neck wounds that are less than 24 hours old.
Patients only need to be hospitalized for human bite wounds if they have evidence of systemic infection, such as fever, progressing lymphangitis, or obvious oral antibiotic failure.
The infection rate can be as high as 47% for human bite wounds if they are not treated with antibiotics. B
Only 10% of patients with metacarpophalangeal septic arthritis from a human bite recover full function. B

Bloodborne pathogen risk associated with human bites is rare. An algorithm aimed at avoiding unnecessary testing while remaining OSHA-compliant has been proposed, including testing all biters and bites for hepatitis B; and all biters for HCV and HIV if there was a "bloody saliva bite". C

feature.caption: Oral Antibiotics for Human Bite.
feature.feature_body:
Antibiotic Adult Dosing Pediatric Dosing
Preferred drug
Amoxicillin-clavulante 875-125 mg twice daily Dosing based on amoxicillin component. 25-45mg/kg/day divided in 2 doses (max 875mg/dose, use 200mg/5ml or 400mg/5ml suspension, or 200mg or 400mg chew tabs) or 20-40mg/kg/day divided 3 in doses (max 500mg/dose, use 125mg/5ml or 250/5ml suspension, or 500mg tablet)
Alternate (for penicillin allergy, or to cover skin flora, Eikenella, and anaerobes)
One of following (good Eikenella and aerobic coverage):
Doxycycline 100 mg twice daily 2.2–4.4mg/kg/day divided in 2 doses (max 200mg/day)
Cefuroxime 500 mg twice daily 20-30mg/kg/day divided in 2 doses (max 500mg/dose)
Ciprofloxacin 500-750mg twice daily Not recommended
Moxifloxacin (monotherapy) 400 mg once daily Not recommended
Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole 1 double-strength tablet twice daily 8-10mg/kg/day of TMP divided in 2 doses (max 160mg/dose)
Plus one of these (good anaerobic coverage)
Metronidazole 500 mg three times daily 30mg/kg/day divided in 3 doses (max 500mg/dose)
Clindamycin 300 mg three times daily 20-30mg/kg/day divided in 3 doses (max 450mg/dose)
